en: Now, therefore, [the rules] based on convention and custom.
(ApDhS 1.1.1.2–3) The consensus of those who know the Dharma is an authority, as are the Vedas.
(ApDhS 1.1.1.4–5) There are four castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
Among them, each preceding one is superior by birth (ApDhS 1.1.6).

For those who are not Śūdras and whose actions are not defective, there is the right to initiation, Vedic study, the establishment of the sacred fires, and the performance of rites that bear fruit (ApDhS 1.1.7).
Service is the duty of the Śūdra toward the other castes.
ApDhS 1.1.1.8: In each preceding stage of life, there is greater supreme bliss.

ApDhS 1.1.1.9: Initiation (*upanayana*) is the sacrament for one seeking knowledge, according to the revealed scripture (*śruti*). ApDhS 1.1.1.10: "The *sāvitrī* is recited from all the Vedas," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Indeed, he who is ignorant enters from darkness into darkness," so says the Brāhmaṇa, "both he who initiates an ignorant person and the ignorant person who is initiated."
ApDhS 1.1.1.12: One should seek out a teacher who is endowed with noble birth and learning, and who is well-composed.
ApDhS 1.1.1.13: And one should seek such a teacher whose knowledge and conduct do not deviate from the sacred laws (*dharma*).
ApDhS 1.1.1.14: He from whom one gathers the *dharmas* is the *ācārya*.
One should never do harm to him;
for he indeed gives birth to that [knowledge] through him.
That is the most excellent birth.
It is the body itself that the mother and father produce.

Ap1.1.1.19: One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring, a Rājanya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn; specifically, a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception, a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. Ap1.1.1.20:
Now follow the optional initiations.
In the seventh [month], for one desiring spiritual luster;
in the eighth, for one desiring long life;
in the ninth, for one desiring splendor.
In the tenth [month], one desiring food; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power;
in the twelfth, one desiring cattle.

Up to the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, up to the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, and up to the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya— before these times there is no lapse, provided he is capable of observing the vows which we shall describe.

ApDhS 1.1.1.28: If the time for the Sāvitrī has passed, he shall observe the student-discipline (*brahmacarya*) pertaining to the three Vedas for one season. ApDhS 1.1.1.29: Now follows the initiation (*upanayana*).
ApDhS 1.1.1.30: After that, there shall be bathing in water for one year. ApDhS 1.1.1.31: Then he may be initiated.
ApDhS 1.1.1.32: Now, in the case of one whose father and grandfather have likewise not been initiated...
Those who are designated as "slayers of Brahmins" (brahmaha) should be avoided; one should shun their arrival, their eating together, and their marriage. (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.1.33)
ApDhS 1.1.1.34: For those who desire it, there is an expiation. ApDhS 1.1.1.35: Just as in the case of the first transgression, so it is for a year.
ApDhS 1.1.1.36: Then follows the initiation (upanayana), and after that, the ritual bathing in water.
Ap1.1.2.1: Having counted each person individually according to the number of years they have passed since initiation (*anupeta*), as many as there may be;
Ap1.1.2.2: [He should purify them] with the seven *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "That which is near and that which is far," with the *yajus-pavitra*, the *sāma-pavitra*, and the *āṅgirasa*;
Ap1.1.2.3: Or alternatively, he may do so with the *vyāhṛtis* alone.
(With the *vyāhṛtis*) Ap1.1.2.4. Now, he is to be initiated (*adhyāpya*).
Ap1.1.2.5. Furthermore, those whose initiation is not remembered from their great-grandfather onwards are designated as "associated with the cremation ground" (*śmaśāna-saṃstutāḥ*).
One should avoid their arrival, eating with them, and marriage. If they so desire, the penance is twelve years of Vedic studenthood (*brahmacarya*) according to the *Traividya* rule;
then follows the initiation (*upanayana*), and thereafter the ritual bathing in water with the *Pāvamānī* verses and others.

ApDhS 1.1.2.7: Now follows the instruction on the Gṛhamedha sacrifice. ApDhS 1.1.2.8: There is no teaching of the Veda. ApDhS 1.1.2.9: Then, for him who returns from that [course], the purificatory rite is as prescribed for the first transgression.
From that point onward, it is according to the original rule.
For one who has been initiated, there is residence as a student (brahmacārin) in the teacher’s household.
ApDhS 1.1.2.12: Forty-eight years.
ApDhS 1.1.2.13–15: Or [the vow may be undertaken] for three-quarters less, for half, or for one-third [of that period].

ApDhS 1.1.2.16: [The teacher shall initiate] at least twelve [pupils]. ApDhS 1.1.2.17–18: There is no fasting for a student of sacred knowledge who is living with his teacher. (This concludes the rules for studentship.)
Ap1.1.2.19: He shall remain dependent on his teacher, except in cases involving acts that cause loss of caste (*patanīya*). Ap1.1.2.20: He should be one who acts for the teacher's welfare.

He should not contradict the speech of his teacher (ApDhS 1.1.2.21); he should remain seated or lying down when the teacher is so (ApDhS 1.1.2.22); and he should not eat food that has been specially prepared for him (ApDhS 1.1.2.23).
Likewise, [he should avoid] alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat;
he should not sleep during the day;
and he should not use perfumes.
26. He shall not engage in sexual intercourse. 27. He shall abandon self-praise. 28. He shall not wash his limbs.
ApDhS 1.1.2.29: He should wash those parts of his body that have been smeared with impurities, provided he is not within the sight of his teacher.
ApDhS 1.1.2.30: He should not bathe in water while praising himself.
If he were to bathe, he would float like a staff. (ApDhS 1.1.2.31–32) [He should be] one with matted hair, with his top-knot matted.
Or he may have others shave [it]; [the girdle] is made of muñja grass. Ap1.1.2.33. muñjī.
ApDhS 1.1.2.34: The girdle of a Kṣatriya is made of bowstring. ApDhS 1.1.2.35: [The girdle] of a Vaiśya is made of muñja grass. ApDhS 1.1.2.36: Or it may be a cord of sheep’s wool for a Vaiśya.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of śirīṣa or palāśa wood; that of a Rājanya is produced from the branch of a nyagrodha tree and is bent downwards.
Some teachers [teach] that for a Vaiśya, the staff is made of bādara or udumbara wood, or that the staff is made of wood regardless of caste;
[they also teach] the garment. ĀpDhS 1.1.2.39.
ApDhS 1.1.2.40: [The garments of the student shall be] made of hemp, linen, or skins.
ApDhS 1.1.2.41: Some teachers prescribe that the garment be dyed reddish-brown (kaṣāya).
ApDhS 1.1.3.1: That of a Kṣatriya [shall be] dyed madder-red (māñjiṣṭha).
The girdle of a Vaiśya is made of hemp.
That of a Brāhmaṇa is made of the skin of a black antelope or a deer;
if it is black, he must not sit or lie down on a spread-out seat.
ApDhS 1.1.3.5: The skin of the Ruru deer for a Kṣatriya.
ApDhS 1.1.3.6: The skin of a goat for a Vaiśya. ApDhS 1.1.3.7–8: The skin of a sheep is permitted for all castes.
"Desiring the prosperity of the Brahman, he should wear only skins; desiring the prosperity of the Kṣatra, only garments; desiring the prosperity of both, both—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
However, he should wear the skin as the upper garment."
ApDhS 1.1.3.11: He shall not look upon improper dancing. ApDhS 1.1.3.12: He shall not go to assemblies or social gatherings. ApDhS 1.1.3.13: He shall not be habituated to gossiping about people.
ApDhS 1.1.3.14: He should be habitually secretive. ApDhS 1.1.3.15: He should not perform independent actions contrary to the conduct of his teacher.
Ap1.1.3.16: He should converse with women only as much as is necessary. Ap1.1.3.17–24: He should be gentle and tranquil.
Self-controlled and possessed of a sense of shame.
Firm in resolve,
untiring, free from anger, and without malice.
Bringing all his gains to the teacher, he should go on his rounds for alms in the evening and morning without reciting mantras; while begging, he should...
"Except for those who are unworthy recipients and those who have been accused;
[one may give] with a vessel (or from one's own hand) to women who refuse [the gift], being composed in mind. (ApDhS 1.1.3.26a)
The student’s sacrifice,
gift,
and oblation.
He appropriates offspring, cattle, spiritual luster, and food;
therefore, one should not refuse a group of students practicing the life of a religious student (*brahmacārin*).
"Indeed, he should be of such a kind and observe such vows among these;
so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Alms are not to be sought by inference, but rather through what is seen and heard. (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.3.27)
A Brāhmaṇa should beg with the word "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Rājanya with the word "bhavat" in the middle;
a Vaiśya with the word "bhavat" at the end.
Ap1.1.3.31: Having collected that and placed it before the teacher, he should announce it to him.
Ap1.1.3.32: He should eat what has been served by him.
ApDhS 1.1.3.33: When separated from his guru, he may seek alms from the family of a teacher.
ApDhS 1.1.3.34: When separated from them as well, he may seek alms from other learned Brahmins (śrotriya).
ApDhS 1.1.3.35: He should not go about for his own sake alone.
ApDhS 1.1.3.36: Having eaten himself, he should wash the vessel. ApDhS 1.1.3.37: And he should not leave it soiled with food remnants. ApDhS 1.1.3.38:
If he is unable to do so, he should bury it in the ground.
Ap1.1.3.39: Or he should cause it to enter into water.
Ap1.1.3.40: Or he should hand it over to a noble Ārya.
Ap1.1.3.41: Or to a Śūdra who acts as an intermediary.
ApDhS 1.1.3.42: One who has gone abroad should eat after having offered alms-food into the fire.
ApDhS 1.1.3.43: Alms-food is declared to be equivalent to an oblation; in that regard, the teacher serves as the deity.
ApDhS 1.1.3.44: And he serves as the Āhavanīya fire.
ApDhS 1.1.3.45: Having fed him, he eats what remains as leavings.
ApDhS 1.1.4.1: That which he eats as leavings— ApDhS 1.1.4.2: that is indeed the leavings of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-ucchiṣṭa*).

Whatever other substances he offers according to what is available, these indeed constitute his sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the sacrifice of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), which is perpetually extended.
And one should not give him leavings that are prohibited by the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
ApDhS 1.1.4.6: For example: "alkali, salt, honey, and meat.
ApDhS 1.1.4.7: By this, other restrictive rules are explained.
ApDhS 1.1.4.8: For direct revelation (śruti) is more authoritative than customary practice (ācāra) based on inference.
And a cause for activity is indeed observed. For pleasure is experienced.
The leftovers of the father and the eldest brother are to be eaten.
ApDhS 1.1.4.12: When there is a conflict regarding dharma, [the food] is not to be eaten.
ApDhS 1.1.4.13: Morning and evening, he should fetch a water-pot.
ApDhS 1.1.4.14: Having always brought firewood from the forest, he should place it below.

ApDhS 1.1.4.15: One should not go out to fetch firewood after the sun has set. ApDhS 1.1.4.16: Having kindled the fire and swept around it, one should place fuel on it in the evening and in the morning, according to the instruction.
ApDhS 1.1.4.17: Some say that the worship of the fire should take place only in the evening.

ApDhS 1.1.4.18: One should stir a kindled fire with the hand, not with a stirring-stick. ApDhS 1.1.4.19: But before that, one may act as one pleases. ApDhS 1.1.4.20: One should not perform useless acts with water remaining from [use for] the sacred fires, nor should one sip water [for *ācamana*] with such water.
ApDhS 1.1.4.21: One should not sip water (perform *ācamana*) with water that has been agitated by the hand, nor with water drawn up by a single hand.
ApDhS 1.1.4.22: And one should avoid sleep.
ApDhS 1.1.4.23: Furthermore, day after day, he should serve his teacher with actions consistent with righteousness (*dharma*) and worldly purpose (*artha*).
Ap1.1.4.24: Having protected [the teacher], while entering [his presence], he should say: "I have protected the guardian of Dharma. Ap1.1.4.25:
If the teacher, whether through negligence or intentionally, violates a rule, he should point it out to him in private.
Ap1.1.4.26–27: If [the teacher] does not desist, he himself should undertake the performance of the duties.
Or he may turn back.
Now, they say that he who rises early and goes to bed late does not sleep.
For a religious student who has thus directed his self, all his actions become fruitful and attained right here.
Even those [duties] which exist in the life of a householder,
the word *tapas* (austerity) refers to the observances (*niyama*). Upon the transgression of these, the sacred knowledge and the ritual action flow out from this person, along with his offspring.
The offspring of one who falls into a pit is short-lived.
Therefore, because of their transgression of the rules, sages are not born among later generations.

However, some become *śruta-ṛṣis* (sages through sacred learning) upon being reborn due to the remainder of the fruits of their past actions, such as Śvetaketu. Whatever one who is concentrated (*samāhita*) meditates upon as Brahman—*ApDhS 1.2.5.5–6*. And whatever he meditates upon with a concentrated mind—that indeed becomes his world after death—*ApDhS 1.2.5.7*.
One employs [the Veda] from the teacher just as one would [employ] the Brahman; in that regard, the fruit comes to be.
Moreover, they teach: "Whatever one intends with the mind, meditates upon with speech, or perceives with the eye—it becomes exactly so. (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.2.5.8)
(Kaṅkhalpyan) "The rites for propitiating the teacher, rites for securing well-being, and the completion of one's studies"— these are the duties;
other duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) cease from this point on.
One who maintains his private Vedic study, delights in dharma, performs austerities, is upright, and gentle—such a student succeeds. (K:
not crooked) Always rising during the latter part of the night, he should stand before his teacher in the morning and offer a respectful greeting, saying: "O sir, I am so-and-so.
(K: the manner of greeting)
And among those residing in the same village, one should rise before the morning meal for others who are senior;
likewise upon returning from a journey when meeting them.
ApDhS 1.2.5.15: One who desires heaven and long life [should do so].
ApDhS 1.2.5.16: A Brāhmaṇa should salute by extending his right arm level with his ear; a Rājanya level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist;
and a Śūdra with his hands joined in *añjali* at a low level.
ApDhS 1.2.5.17: And there shall be the immersion of the name, as well as the salutation and the return-salutation for the preceding castes.
ApDhS 1.2.5.18: But when the sun has risen, having met with the teacher, there shall be the clasping of his feet. ApDhS 1.2.5.19: There shall always be the salutation.
Ap1.2.5.20: "Having grasped [the feet], [one says] 'Teacher,' so say some.
Ap1.2.5.21: With his right hand, having touched the right foot from below including the instep, he should grasp it.
Ap1.2.5.22: Both [feet] should be grasped by both [hands] while pressing them; so say some."
Ap1.2.5.23: One who is well-engaged [in study] throughout the entire day shall not recite immediately after [such engagement], but rather after a break from study.
Ap1.2.5.24: Likewise, one shall not recite while performing services for the teacher.
Ap1.2.5.25: And one shall not recite even mentally during a time when study is prohibited.
And he should be one who studies when called upon.
He should always cause his teacher to lie down at night, having washed his feet and massaged them.
Having been permitted, he should lie down himself.
And one should not stretch out toward him (Ap 1.2.6.3). Some say that there is no stretching out while sitting on a couch (Ap 1.2.6.4).
Nor should one speak while lying down in his presence (Ap 1.2.6.5).
When addressed, one should respond while remaining seated; when he stands up, one should not rise after him;
when he walks away, one should follow after him.
One should run after someone who is running (ApDhS 1.2.6.10).

One should not sit down wearing sandals, nor with one's head wrapped [in a cloth], nor with hands tucked under the armpits (ApDhS 1.2.6.11). However, one who has set out on a journey or is engaged in work may sit down.

Ap1.2.6.12: Unless he sits down [to study], he should attend upon the teacher as if he were a god. Ap1.2.6.13: Without speaking ill [of him] and without being dejected in mind, he should listen to his speech with a desire to hear. Ap1.2.6.14: He should not sit with his knees drawn up toward his chest.
Ap1.2.6.15–17: [When the wind] blows along [the body], when it has passed by,
when it is not obstructed by the hand,
and when it does not rest upon [the body]— except in other cases.
(ApDhS 1.2.6.18) When the wind blows from behind,
one who wears two garments should wear the sacrificial thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī).
(ApDhS 1.2.6.19) But when wearing only one garment, he should wear it below the navel (adho-nivītaḥ).

Ap1.2.6.20: [The word *abhimukha*] is used [as a karmapravacanīya] with that which is not facing it (*anabhimukham*). Ap1.2.6.21: [The word *anāsanna*] is used [as a karmapravacanīya] with that which is not too near and not too far (*anatidūre*). (K: and also with that which is not too far).
Ap1.2.6.22: [As far as he can reach with his arms while sitting];
Ap1.2.6.23: [not against the wind];
Ap1.2.6.24–25: A student of a single chapter should sit down facing the right arm.
Many [may stand] according to available space (Ap 1.2.6.26).
When [the teacher] stands, [the pupil] shall not sit, nor engage in reclining or sitting (Ap 1.2.6.27). And when [the teacher] is seated, he shall not lie down.
28. And he should exert himself when desiring to act within the scope of that capacity.
29. And he should not show deference to one who stands in his presence as a subordinate.
Or one may mention him by his lineage.
One should not rise up toward him, nor should one rise up after him.
Even if his teacher should be present, (31–32) he should rise from his seat and move away from his place.
(32) Some say that he should address even his own teacher who is a pupil of that [other] teacher by name, as "my teacher. (33)
ApDhS 1.2.6.35: But toward one who is not related to him as a teacher, yet toward whom he behaves with respect, even if that person is merely a junior, he should behave as toward a teacher.
ApDhS 1.2.6.36–37: Having eaten in his presence, he should not rise after him nor give him his leftovers; or, he may rinse his mouth (*ācamet*).
Ap1.2.6.38: Having addressed him with "What shall I do? (or "I shall rise," or "I shall remain silent"), he should rise, or else remain silent.
(K 37) Ap1.2.7.1: He should rise, or else remain silent. Ap1.2.7.2: He should not turn his back on the teacher; having circumambulated him clockwise, he should depart.

ApDhS 1.2.7.3: One should not look at a naked woman. ApDhS 1.2.7.4: Having plucked [a part] from herbs or trees, one should not smell it. ApDhS 1.2.7.5: One should avoid sandals, an umbrella, and a vehicle.
ApDhS 1.2.7.6: He shall not smile. ApDhS 1.2.7.7: If he should smile, he should do so covering his mouth; for thus says the Brāhmaṇa. ApDhS 1.2.7.8: He shall not kiss a woman with his mouth.
Ap1.2.7.9: One should not make a request with the heart.
Ap1.2.7.10: One should not touch [water] without a reason.
Ap1.2.7.11: "One who is in the menses or has blood on the teeth should speak the truth," for so says the Brāhmaṇa.
ApDhS 1.2.7.12: Those who are the lineage-successors of his teacher in that particular branch of knowledge which he practices under him are also his teachers.
ApDhS 1.2.7.13: When he sees others whom he should otherwise greet by clasping their feet, they must then be greeted by clasping their feet.
ApDhS 1.2.7.14: When a multitude of teachers is present and alms have been obtained, the alms belong to the one whom he follows.
Upon merely returning from his studies, he should give [the gift];
the mother should cause him to go to the husband; the husband [should cause him] to go to the teacher.
ApDhS 1.2.7.18: Or he may employ it for religious duties.
ApDhS 1.2.7.19: Having acquired as much learning as he is able, he should, according to his ability and in accordance with the law, bring the Vedic teacher’s fee.
ApDhS 1.2.7.20: But if the teacher is in distress, he may obtain it from a fierce person or from a Śūdra.
ApDhS 1.2.7.21: Some maintain that it is lawful to obtain the teacher's fee at any time from a Śūdra or an Ugra.
ApDhS 1.2.7.22: Having given it, one should not speak of it again.
ApDhS 1.2.7.23: Having performed [the service], one should not recall it again.

One should avoid self-praise and the censure of others. When commanded, one should perform exactly that which was assigned. Furthermore, in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction from the teacher, one’s conduct should follow other [established rules].
ApDhS 1.2.7.27: Except for clasping the feet and eating the remnants of his food, one’s conduct toward the teacher’s wife is the same as toward the teacher.
ApDhS 1.2.7.28: Likewise toward one who instructs him [in the Veda] or teaches him [the Veda].
ApDhS 1.2.7.29: And likewise toward a fellow student who is older than oneself.

ApDhS 1.2.7.30: One should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself, with the exception of eating his leftovers. ApDhS 1.2.7.31: Even for one who has returned home from studentship (*samāvṛtta*), this same conduct applies according to traditional custom. ApDhS 1.2.8.1: It is exactly like the conduct prescribed for the religious student (*brahmacārin*).

Ap1.2.8.2: Wearing garlands, having smeared one's face, having anointed one's hair and beard, being anointed, being rubbed with unguents, wearing a turban or a head-wrap, wearing a tunic, and wearing sandals— Ap1.2.8.3:
He should neither perform nor cause these things to be performed during the sacred observances (*udācāra*).
Ap1.2.8.4: Nor should he do so during acts of self-will (*svairi-karman*).
ApDhS 1.2.8.5: For example, [the teacher should not mention] the washing of teeth, anointing, or scraping [the tongue].

ApDhS 1.2.8.6: Nor should the teacher mention the substances used for those acts when they have been employed on his own person. ApDhS 1.2.8.7: But when he has bathed at the proper time, whether the materials have been brought according to rule, or he has been invited, or has come of his own accord, some say that he should not withdraw them.
One should not sit higher than [the teacher], nor on a seat with many legs, nor on anything that is firmly established on all sides.
ApDhS 1.2.8.11: One should not sit upon a bed or a seat that has been used by another. ApDhS 1.2.8.12: When commanded while on a journey, one may mount a vehicle after the other. ApDhS 1.2.8.13:
And likewise a council hall, a touchstone, a mat, or a grass mat.

ApDhS 1.2.8.14: One should not speak to one's teacher unless addressed first, except for words of affection. ApDhS 1.2.8.15: One should avoid poking at him, whispering against him, laughing loudly in his presence, calling out to him, mentioning his name, and giving him commands. ApDhS 1.2.8.16: In times of distress, one may make oneself known for the sake of a necessary purpose.
ApDhS 1.2.8.17: Living together, he should go to see his teacher every evening and morning, even if unsummoned.
ApDhS 1.2.8.18: And having stayed away from home, he should see him on that very day.
ApDhS 1.2.8.19–20: When the teacher and the sub-teacher meet, he should first clasp the feet of the sub-teacher and then desire to clasp the feet of the teacher.
Another may deny the teacher;
however, in his presence, honor is lost. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.57–58)
He should go frequently to the teacher’s household for the purpose of seeing him, bringing as much as he is able—down to even tooth-cleansing sticks—as a gift.
(K inserts: One should not approach one's mother, father, teacher, the sacred fires, or the houses with empty hands; nor should one approach a king without having studied [the Vedas].
Regarding that [teacher], this is the conduct toward the guru. (K 24)
Desiring him as if he were his own son, and not concealing anything regarding all duties, the teacher, being well-disciplined, should cause him to grasp the knowledge.

And he should not obstruct him with obstacles to study for the sake of his own interests, except in times of distress. One who fails to apply himself skillfully toward the teacher becomes a non-pupil despite being a pupil, having failed to properly dedicate himself to the teacher.
ApDhS 1.2.8.27: Even a teacher ceases to be a teacher if he neglects what he has heard [from the scriptures].

(K 28) ApDhS 1.2.8.28: And one should constantly reprove him for his transgressions. (K 29) ApDhS 1.2.8.29: Intimidation, fasting, touching water, and exclusion from sight are the punishments, applied according to the gravity of the offense, until desistance occurs. (K 30)

Ap1.2.8.30: Having completed his period of celibacy (*caritabrahmacarya*) and having withdrawn from other religious duties, he should grant permission [to study], saying, "Be present [for study] immediately. Ap1.3.9.1: Having performed the commencement of the term (*upākarma*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the first watch of the night for one month.
