Even when one cannot subsist by one's own means, one may enjoy [the land] after giving gold or a cow.
One must not settle there permanently.
Having obtained a means of livelihood, he should desist from further study.
One who has returned home from his teacher (samāvṛtta) must not eat food provided by members of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya.
By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa may be eaten; it becomes inedible only for a specific reason.
(K bhoktavyam akāraṇād) Ap1.6.18.11:
Where one performs an act that requires penance without having performed the penance, (Ap1.6.18.12: food may be eaten from one who has completed the penance).
Ap1.6.18.12: Food may be eaten from one who has performed the penance.

ApDhS 1.6.18.13: Some say that one may eat the food of all social classes (*varṇas*) provided they abide by their own respective duties, with the exception of a *śūdra*. ApDhS 1.6.18.14: Even for such a *śūdra*, however, if he has acquired wealth through righteous means (*dharmopanatasya*), one may eat. ApDhS 1.6.18.15: Having given gold or a cow, one may eat; one should not settle there permanently, but having obtained a livelihood, one should desist.
The food of a guild (saṅgha) is unfit to be eaten; likewise that which is offered by calling out to the public; and the food of all those who subsist by manual crafts.
Those who live by the sword; those who live by usury;
and physicians.
A usurer;
one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice but has not yet purchased the King Soma; and [one who is impure] only until the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya rite.
Ap1.6.18.25: Or, once the omentum has been offered, the initiated person may eat.
Ap1.6.18.26: Or, when that which is designated for the sake of the sacrifice has been consumed, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the Brāhmaṇa. Ap1.6.18.27: A eunuch.
One who carries out the commands of kings;
one who does not perform sacrifices with sacrificial oblations (havis);
one who is a spy.
And one who has gone forth as a renunciant without following the prescribed rule;
and he who abandons the sacred fires;
and he who avoids all [Vedic study]; and a Śrotriya who is excluded from the community; and the husband of a Śūdra woman.

ApDhS 1.6.19.1: One who is intoxicated, insane, bound, lacking a retinue, or one who has sat down in protest, as well as one who causes another to sit down in protest—[these shall not eat] for that duration of time.
ApDhS 1.6.19.2: Who is his food?
ApDhS 1.6.19.3: "Whoever desires it," says Kaṇva.
"It is meritorious," says Kautsa. "Whoever may give [it]," says Vārṣyāyaṇi.
"If the impurity (*rajas*) in a person is stationary, it must be experienced; but if it is mobile, one becomes free from fault through giving. (K)
ApDhS 1.6.19.7: Pure alms-food is to be eaten by the Eka-kuṇika, as well as by the followers of Kāṇva and Kutsa, and likewise by Puṣkarasādin.
ApDhS 1.6.19.8: That which is endowed with everything is the rule of Vārṣyāyaṇi.
(Endowed with everything)
Double sandhi?
Ap1.6.19.9: Of that which is desired as merit, one should eat.
Ap1.6.19.10: Even of that which is not desired as merit, one should not eat.
"Food may be eaten from anyone whatsoever.
"Not unless it has been previously offered," says Hārīta.
Now, they cite two verses from the Purāṇas:
"Prajāpati considered alms that have been offered, brought forward, and announced beforehand as fit to be eaten even by one who has committed evil deeds."
"The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who holds her in contempt."
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch— these are not to be eaten.
(Kṣaṇḍaka’s):
Furthermore, they also cite this:
“The killer of a learned Brahmin transfers his guilt to the eater of his food; the innocent man he falsely accuses.”
A thief released by the king, having made a request, is defiled by falsehood.
One should not practice religious duties by placing this worldly purpose before oneself;
for they become fruitless with respect to spiritual elevation (*abhyudaya*).
Just as when a tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary effects.
Thus, while practicing the Dharma in this way, benefits arise;
if they do not arise, there is no loss of Dharma. One should be free from envy and difficult to deceive regarding the talk of deceivers, rogues, nihilists, and fools.
"Neither do we two move about as Dharma and Adharma," nor do the gods, Gandharvas, or ancestors declare, "This is Dharma; this is Adharma.
Rather, that which the Āryas praise while it is being performed is Dharma, and that which they censure is Adharma.
ApDhS 1.7.20.8: In all countries, he should adopt the conduct of those Āryas who are exclusively concentrated, well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy.
ApDhS 1.7.20.9: In this way, he conquers both worlds.
ApDhS 1.7.20.10: Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa.
In times of distress, he may trade while excluding those goods that are forbidden for sale:

human beings, liquids, dyes, perfumes, food, hides, a cow that has recently calved, phlegm, water, young sprouts, fermenting agents, long pepper and black pepper, grain, meat, weapons, and the hope for a good reward.

One should especially not sell sesame and rice among grains. Furthermore, the mutual exchange of these is not prescribed. Nor should there be an exchange of food for food, of humans for humans, of liquids for liquids, of fragrances for fragrances, or of knowledge for knowledge.
One should engage in trade with goods that have not been purchased:
with *muñja* grass, *balbaja* grass, roots, and fruits; and with grass and wood that have not been processed.
One should not settle down permanently [in one place].
Having obtained a livelihood, one should desist [from worldly activity].
No social intercourse with outcasts is permitted.
Likewise, [one is excluded] by those who have lost their ritual vessels (ApDhS 1.7.21.6).
Now, [follow] the causes for loss of caste (patanīya):

theft, false accusation, killing a human being, abandoning a Veda-student, causing an abortion, sexual intercourse with the mother, with the paternal aunt, with a female relative within the prohibited degree of kinship, with offspring, or with a woman, as well as the drinking of *surā* liquor (ApDhS 1.7.21.7–8).
[This is] the union of the ununited.

(ApDhS 1.7.21.9) Having approached a heavy female friend, a friend of a teacher, and other wives of others, some say that one does not fall [from his caste] unless it be the wife of a Guru. (ApDhS 1.7.21.10)
But the constant practice of unrighteous acts [is a cause of impurity].
Now, the things that cause impurity:
sexual intercourse with an Ārya woman by a Śūdra.
[The eating of the meat of] prohibited animals;
[the meat] of dogs, humans, domestic cocks and pigs, and carnivorous beasts;
and the consumption of the urine and excrement of humans.
Eating the leavings of a Śūdra and the acceptance of vessels from outcasts are [grounds for loss of caste] for Āryas.
Some say that these also are causes of falling [from caste].
Therefore, other [acts] are defective and cause impurity.

(ApDhS 1.7.21.19) Having recognized a fault, one should not be the first to proclaim it to others regarding one who has fallen; rather, one should avoid him in religious duties. (ApDhS 1.7.21.20) One should practice spiritual disciplines that are consistent with justice and free from worldly distraction. (ApDhS 1.8.22.1)
Ap1.8.22.2: There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self.
Ap1.8.22.3: In this regard, we shall cite verses concerning the attainment of the Self. Ap1.8.22.4:
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18) All living beings are indeed the city of Him who dwells in the cave of the heart.
Those who practice that which is unshakable, yet has its abode in the mobile world— being themselves unslain and free from stain— they are immortal. That which is here,
in this very world, is called the object of the senses.
Having shaken off this [world], the wise man should attend to that which lies hidden within.
Not finding the "I" in the self alone, practice what is beneficial and not what is harmful. Furthermore, I shall seek the state of the virtuous among others without expectation.
The great body of splendor, the Lord established everywhere—
He who is eternal among all beings, the wise, the immortal, and the firm; bodiless, soundless, formless, intangible, yet great and pure.
He is everything, the ultimate limit, and indeed the equinox; whoever should follow him would always act with devotion toward him everywhere.
One who is disciplined shall behold that which is difficult to see and subtle, and he shall rejoice in the world.
Seeing all beings in the Self and contemplating thus, the wise man should not be deluded;
he who sees the Self everywhere indeed shines as Brahmā upon the back of the firmament.

He who is subtle, subtler than the finest fiber of a lotus stalk, and who stands pervading all; who is greater than the earth, firm, and who stands supporting all— he is the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), distinct from the knowledge of this world by means of the senses, yet not different from that which is to be known, and he is the one who apportions.
From that all bodies arise; it is the root, eternal and permanent.
But in this life, the eradication of faults has its root in yoga;
having removed those things that burn living beings, the wise man attains security.
Now we shall set forth the defects that lead to the destruction of beings:
anger, joy, wrath, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, gluttony, slander, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga; the eradication of these is rooted in yoga.
Freedom from anger, freedom from joy, freedom from wrath, freedom from greed, freedom from delusion, freedom from hypocrisy, freedom from malice, and truthful speech.
Moderation in eating, absence of backbiting, freedom from envy, sharing, renunciation, straightforwardness, gentleness, tranquility, self-control, non-opposition toward all beings,
yoga, nobility, kindness, and contentment— these are the rules of conduct for all stages of life; by practicing them according to the prescribed rule, one becomes a traveler to all goals.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a thousand cows as a means of expiation for the enmity;
a hundred for a Vaiśya, and ten for a Śūdra.
And in every case, an additional bull is required for the purpose of atonement.

And with respect to women, it is the same for these [offenses]. Having killed a student of the Veda belonging to either of the two former castes, or one who has entered a sacrificial session (*savana*), or even a mere Brāhmaṇa, he is accused (*abhiśasta*).
And [the killing of] an embryo whose sex is unknown, and [the killing of] a woman who has recently borne a child (an ātreyī)—
the expiation for that is as follows.

ApDhS 1.9.24.11: Having built a hut in the forest, restrained in speech, bearing a corpse's head as his banner, and having covered himself with half a garment of hemp from below the navel to above the knees;
ApDhS 1.9.24.12: His path shall be between the two tracks of the road.
ApDhS 1.9.24.13: And upon seeing another person, he should step aside.
With a broken red earthen bowl, he should enter a village.
He should wander for alms among seven houses, saying, "Alms for one accused."
That is the mode of subsistence.
Having not obtained [the means for a fast],
he should tend cattle.
Regarding them, their going out and entering a village constitutes a second offense.
Having practiced this for twelve years, he attains communion with the virtuous.
Or, having built a hut on the path of a battle, he may dwell there desiring to win over Brahmins and cattle; having been thrice defeated, or having failed to win, he is released.

Or, having performed the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, he is released. In a conflict between *dharma* and *artha*, this same penance applies to one who chooses *artha*.
Having killed a teacher or a *śrotriya* who has completed his ritual duties, he shall perform this very rite until his last breath.
For him, there is no return to this world; rather, his defilement is destroyed.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place them in his cupped hands, and walk toward the southern direction from which there is no return.
Or, he may embrace a glowing iron image of a woman and meet his end.
If one touches liquor with water, one should drink liquor.

A thief, with his hair disheveled, should go to the king carrying a club upon his shoulder and confess his deed; the king should strike him with it, and by that blow, he is released from the offense. (Having placed the club on him,) he should be struck.
If he permits [the act],
sin touches the one who permits it.
Or he should enter the fire, or undertake severe austerity.

Or he may attain purification by reducing his food intake; or he may perform the Kṛcchra-saṃvatsara penance. Furthermore, they also cite this: ApDhS 1.9.25.7–10: "By the reduction of his food, he may attain purification for himself; or he may perform the Kṛcchra-saṃvatsara. Now, they also quote:"

Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or violated the teacher’s wife— even if they have not committed the murder of a Brahmin— they should eat measured food at the fourth mealtime and descend into water according to the ritual for the *savanas*.
By alternating between standing and sitting, they remove their sin after three years.
Having omitted the first social class [from his intent], having slain the first social class, he should go to battle;
there they shall kill him.
Or else, having caused his hair, skin, and flesh to be offered as an oblation, he should enter the fire.

ApDhS 1.9.25.13: For killing a crow, a peacock, a peacock-of-the-forest (*barhiṇa*), a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), a swan (*haṃsa*), a vulture (*bhāsa*), a frog, a mongoose, a *ḍerika*, or a horse, the penance is the same as that for a Śūdra. ( = K 14) ApDhS 1.9.26.1: And likewise for killing a milch-cow or a bull without cause. ApDhS 1.9.26.2: And for causing the death of other draft animals or living beings [used for labor].
ApDhS 1.9.26.3: Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken an untruth, one shall subsist for three nights on food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salty.
ApDhS 1.9.26.4: For a Śūdra, there shall be fasting for seven nights.
ApDhS 1.9.26.5: And the same applies to women.
ApDhS 1.9.26.6: For those offenses involving formal accusation, one limb shall be cut off, provided there is no injury to life.

ApDhS 1.9.26.7: Having committed acts such as ignoble speech, calumny, and forbidden conduct; having consumed what is unfit to be eaten, tasted, or drunk; having shed semen in a Śūdra woman or in a non-vaginal opening; and having performed a blameworthy act either intentionally or unintentionally—[one must perform penance].
Or he should touch water with verses addressed to Vāyu, or with those addressed to Varuṇa, or with other purificatory mantras, according to the repetition of the rite.
One who has committed the *avakīrṇin* offense should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using the *pākayajña* ritual.

A Śūdra shall eat of that [remnant]. (ApDhS 1.9.26.9) [This is] the penance for studying falsely. (ApDhS 1.9.26.10) Or, remaining devoted to the welfare of his teacher for one year, he shall restrain his speech, except when reciting the Veda; the teacher [shall do the same], as well as toward the teacher’s wife and while wandering for alms. (ApDhS 1.9.26.11)
In this same manner, regarding other sinful acts involving self-degradation (*svapātanīya*) which we shall describe later:
one should either offer oblations with the words "Desire has done it" or "Anger has done it," or one should mutter them.

Alternatively, on a sacred festival day (*parvan*), having fasted while subsisting on sesame seeds, or having fasted on the following day, one should touch water and repeat the *Sāvitrī* mantra a thousand times, either accompanied by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) or without breath-control.

On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having fasted while subsisting on sesame seeds, or on the following day, having touched the water of a great river, one should offer a thousand pieces of fuel wood with the Sāvitrī mantra or recite it;
or one should perform purificatory *iṣṭi* sacrifices, *yajña*s, or *kratu*s.
ApDhS 1.9.27.3: Having eaten food that is unfit to be eaten, one becomes free from excrement.
ApDhS 1.9.27.4: That state is attained within seven nights.
ApDhS 1.9.27.5: Or, during both the morning and evening twilights of the winter and cool seasons, one should touch water.
(Or, at the two twilights) he may perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance.

The rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* is as follows: for three days he eats only what is not prepared with oil; for the next three days he eats only during the daytime; for the following three days he observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for; and for the final three days he does not eat anything at all.
One should practice this very same [penance] for one year; that is the *saṃvatsara-kṛcchra*. Now, another [method]:
even after committing many acts that cause loss of caste (*apatana*), one becomes purified by having performed the penance through three recitations of the Veda while fasting.
Furthermore, many... (K 1: ...; 2: not eating). Ap1.9.27.10:
(Ś) If he should support an ignoble woman on his bed, he should increase his ascetic heat by drinking astringent decoctions;
like a non-Brahmin, having paid homage, he should sit upon blades of grass with his back scorched by the sun. (K *bibhart*); Ap1.9.27.10: (Ś) *bibhret*.
Whatever black sin a Brāhmaṇa incurs by associating with the dark caste for a single night,
he destroys that sin in three years by eating only at the fourth mealtime and subsisting on water.
"Whoever considers the property of another as his own becomes a thief," so say Kautsa, Hārīta, Kaṇva, and Puṣkarasādi.
Vārṣyāyaṇi says that there are exceptions regarding the taking of certain things. Chaff, fodder for draft animals, and food do not prohibit one from taking them from their owners.
Excessive taking away results in failure.
Hārīta says that in all cases it must be preceded by permission. One should not go to see an outcast teacher or a kinsman.
And he should not enjoy these pleasures;
having accepted what comes by chance, he should pass by in silence.
A mother undertakes many actions for the sake of her sonhood.
In her case, service should be rendered constantly even if she has fallen from grace;
however, there should be no joint performance of religious duties (*dharma-saṃnipāta*). (Or: there should be no cohabitation.)

Having permitted himself enjoyments acquired through unrighteousness, and having declared, "Neither we nor unrighteousness," he shall cover the area from below the navel to above the knees, touch water at the three times of day (*triṣavaṇa*), eat food that is neither milk, nor pungent, nor salty, and for twelve years he shall not enter a house.
(1: Not [looking] downward;
2: Covering the knees; 3: [Avoiding] alkaline salt; 4: Not [entering] a house.)
From that, success follows.
Now, as for association with the noble ones:
this same [principle] applies to other acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) as well.
But one who has violated the teacher’s bed shall enter a hollow metal image (*sūrmi*), set it ablaze at both ends, and burn himself therein.
Hārīta says this is false;
for he who regards himself as another—or another as himself—is indeed already accursed.
By this very rule, one should proceed until the final exhalation; for him,
there is no returning to this world,
but his defilement is indeed cast out.
ApDhS 1.10.28.19: One who has committed adultery shall put on a donkey skin with the hair turned outward and beg for alms, saying, "Alms for one who has committed adultery," at seven houses;
that is his mode of subsistence for six months.
But in the case of a woman who has committed adultery with her husband, there shall be a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance repeated for that same duration of time.

Now, a slayer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*), having put on either a dog's skin or a donkey's skin with the hair turned outward, and having taken a human head for the purpose of drinking [the blood] against the current [of the river], [shall perform the penance].
Carrying a cot-leg as a staff and announcing his occupation by name, he should wander about, saying, "Who will give alms to a killer of an embryo?
Having obtained the means of subsistence in a village, he should take refuge in an empty house or at the root of a tree, for he has no association with noble men (*āryas*).
By this very same procedure, one should practice until the final breath;
for him there is no restoration to his former status in this world,
but his defilement is indeed removed.
He who, being negligent, kills one who has arrived [as his victim], incurs the fruit of the sin along with his intention;
the same applies to other sinful actions as well.

Likewise, even for the sake of meritorious acts, a Brāhmaṇa should not take up a weapon, even for the purpose of testing it. For in the Purāṇa it is said: "He who strikes one who has already attacked him for the purpose of violence—anger merely touches anger; there is no fault in that."

ApDhS 1.10.29.8: Now, those who have been accused of a crime may live together in community, resolving that they shall act in accordance with the Dharma; they may perform sacrifices for one another, teach one another, and intermarry among themselves.
ApDhS 1.10.29.9: Having produced sons, they should say: "O Brahmin, depart from us; for thus have our noble ancestors conducted themselves toward us."
(K reads *viprajāta* instead of *vipravrajatāt*) ApDhS 1.10.29.10:
Moreover, even one who is not possessed of his senses does not fall [from his caste].
11: This is to be understood by this [very fact].
"For one who is deficient in a limb indeed gives birth to one who is complete in limbs.
"This is false," says Hārīta.
"A woman possesses the same characteristics as a curd-pot."

For when one churns milk that has been curdled with impure curds, no religious duty (*dharma-kṛtya*) is accomplished by that act. Likewise, there is no association with that which is impure once it has been transformed into something pure. (K:
*ātañcya*) Malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and curses (*anuvyāhāra*) cause impurity, yet they do not entail loss of caste (*apatanīya*).
Hārīta says that these two are causes for falling [from caste]. However, one who follows the conduct leading to such a fall becomes impure for twelve months,
twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of seven days, twelve periods of three days, or for twelve days and seven days.
Three days, one day;
(K 1 inserts "twelve days" between "three days" and "twelve days";
K 2 inserts "two days").
Thus ends the expiation for acts causing impurity, according to the repetition of the act.
"By means of knowledge he bathes," say some;
likewise, "by means of a vow of forty-eight years' duration";
and "by means of both knowledge and the vow," say others.
ApDhS 1.11.30.4: In all of these cases, the conduct is that of a *snātaka*.
ApDhS 1.11.30.5: Due to differences in concentration and differences in the sacred texts (*śruti*), there is a difference in the fruit regarding the act of worship.
ApDhS 1.11.30.6: Now, the vows of the *snātaka*.
One should practice exiting and entering villages by the eastern gate, or else by the northern one. At both twilights, one should sit outside the village, restraining one's speech.
In case of a conflict between a scriptural rule and a traditional custom, the one characterized by direct revelation (śruti) is more authoritative.
One should avoid all dyed garments; likewise, one should avoid a garment that is naturally black. One should wear a garment that does not shine brightly.
And one should not cover the head during the day when one is capable of doing otherwise, except during the act of voiding urine or excrement. However,
while voiding urine or excrement, one should do so after covering the head and having placed something over the ground.
One should avoid performing the act of voiding urine or excrement in the shade (of a tree). However, one may void urine in one's own shadow.
One should not void urine or excrement while wearing shoes, nor on ploughed land, on a path, or in water.
Likewise, one should avoid performing the acts of spitting and sexual intercourse in water.
(ApDhS 1.11.30.19) One should avoid facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, or deities while performing the acts of voiding urine or excrement.
(ApDhS 1.11.30.20) For the cleansing after voiding urine or excrement, one should avoid using a stone, a clod of earth, fresh herbs, or trees by tearing off their upright parts. (ApDhS 1.11.30.21)
One should not, within the range of one's power, turn away from fire, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, deities, a door, and a favorable wind.
(K 25; K 1 inserts *ādityam* and *devatādvāram*)
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"One should eat food facing the east; one should discharge excrement facing the south; one should urinate facing the north; and the washing of the feet should be done facing the west."
One should void urine and feces far from one's dwelling, toward the southern direction or slightly southward. After sunset,
one should avoid the act of voiding urine and feces outside the village or far from one's dwelling.
One who is impure should avoid pronouncing the name of a deity (ApDh 1.11.31.4);
likewise, one should avoid mentioning a person when both deities and a king are present (ApDh 1.11.31.5);
and one should avoid touching the feet of a Brāhmaṇa or a cow (ApDh 1.11.31.6).
One should not touch a cow with the hand without a reason; one should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial fees, and virgins;
and one should not point out a cow that is licking [the calf].
[One should not call a cow] "mixed" with its calf except when there is a specific reason. One should not say of a non-milch cow, "she is a non-milch cow";
rather, one should say, "she is one that will become a milch cow."
One should not say "bhadra, bhadra"; rather, one should say "puṇya" or "praśasta. Furthermore, one should not walk over a rope to which a calf is tied.
One should not pass between the two *pleṅkha* beams.
One should not say, "This one is my rival.
If one were to say, "This one is my rival," he would produce a hateful enemy.
One should not say to another, "It is a rainbow" (*indra-dhanuḥ*).
One should not look at falling objects.
One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting.

By day the sun protects living beings, and by night the moon; therefore, on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should desire greater protection for oneself through self-restraint, the period of celibacy, and proper conduct.
For on this night, the sun and the moon dwell together. One should not enter a village by a secret or forbidden path.
If he should enter, he should recite this verse, "Homage to Rudra Vāstoṣpati," or another verse addressed to Rudra.
One should not give the remains of food to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa; if he should give them, he should first scrape off the pieces with his teeth and place them in that person's mouth before giving.
He should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. (ApDhS 1.11.31.23) One engaged in sacred study should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn.
(ApDhS 1.11.32.1) Having engaged in sexual union, he should not sleep with her for the entire night. (ApDhS 1.11.32.2)
3. While lying down, he should avoid teaching. 4. He should not teach on that same bed upon which he himself lies down. 5.
He should not wear visible garlands or apply visible ointments.
32.6. He should always adorn himself for his wife during the night. 32.7. He should avoid immersing his head in water. 32.8. And he should not bathe after sunset.
He should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, wooden sandals, and the cleaning of his teeth.
He should also avoid praising his teacher in his presence, such as saying, "How well you have bathed!
He should remain awake until nightfall.

ApDhS 1.11.32.12: There is no study during the night, except for the instruction of students in the Dharma. ApDhS 1.11.32.13: Or one may study it oneself mentally. ApDhS 1.11.32.14: Teaching [the Veda] takes place after midnight.

ApDhS 1.11.32.15: Having risen after the latter part of the night, one should not go back to bed thinking, "It is a time unfit for study. ApDhS 1.11.32.16: One may, however, lie down on one's side. ApDhS 1.11.32.17: Or one may recite mentally.
He should not frequent low-born people, nor regions inhabited by low-born people; nor should he attend assemblies or social gatherings.
If he must go to a social gathering, he should depart after circumambulating it clockwise.
He should avoid entering cities and should not answer questions. Furthermore,
they also cite this:
"Root and tuft—these uproot the one who speaks ill; they destroy his offspring, cattle, and his dwelling.
O Dharmaprahlāda, weeping for no cause, Death has indeed answered the question. Thus he spoke.
He should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle, as well as ascending or descending uneven places. He should also avoid crossing a river by means of his arms alone.
And one should not board a boat whose safety is doubtful.
One should not cut grass, crush clods of earth, or spit without a valid reason.
And whatever else they censure, and whatever else they censure.
ApDhS 2.1.1.1: From the taking of the hand [in marriage] onwards, there is the vow for the two householders.
ApDhS 2.1.1.2: Eating at the two [prescribed] times.
ApDhS 2.1.1.3: And non-satiety with food.
Ap2.1.1.4: On the festival days (parvan), there shall be fasting for both [husband and wife]. Ap2.1.1.5: The term "fasting" (aupavasta) refers to eating at another time [after the fast].
Ap2.1.1.6: And there must be satisfaction with food.
Ap2.1.1.7: And whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day; Ap2.1.1.8: and they should sleep on the ground;
Ap2.1.1.9: and there shall be abstinence from sexual intercourse.
Ap2.1.1.10: On the following day, there is the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). Ap2.1.1.11: Its procedure is explained by [the rules of] the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice. Ap2.1.1.12:
People prescribe this as a constant rite.
Ap2.1.1.13: Wherever one intends to kindle the fire, there one should draw three lines each toward the east and three toward the north, sprinkle them with water, and then kindle the fire.
Ap2.1.1.14: Having poured out this water, one should place another vessel to the north or to the east.
Ap2.1.1.15: Water-vessels must always remain unfilled with water; this is the vow of the householder and his wife.
ApDhS 2.1.1.16: On the day [of the vow], one should not sleep during the daytime.
ApDhS 2.1.1.17: And during the fertile period, he should unite with his wife according to the prescribed rule.
ApDhS 2.1.1.18: Even during the intervening periods, he should unite only with his wife.

Ap2.1.1.19: And the act of sexual union is permitted by the word of a Brāhmaṇa. Ap2.1.1.20: The actual contact should take place with her wearing only her woman’s garment. Ap2.1.1.21: And they should share the same bed only for as long as the sexual union lasts.
Ap2.1.1.22: After that, [the teacher says] "Nānā" (Separate).
Ap2.1.1.23: [The students] perform the ritual sipping of water (*udaka-upasparśana*).
Ap2.1.2.1: Or rather, having washed the smears and sipped water, there is the sprinkling of the limbs.
Ap2.1.2.2: For all social classes (*varṇa*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*).

Ap2.1.2.3: Thereafter, upon returning [to birth], one obtains—by virtue of the remainder of the fruits of one's actions—one’s caste, form, class, strength, intelligence, wisdom, possessions, and the performance of duty.
Like that wheel, it proceeds only for the sake of happiness in both worlds.
Just as there is an increase in the growth of the fruit of medicinal herbs and trees through the excellence of the seed, the field, and the cultivation, so too is it here.
By this, the increase of the fruit of faults has been explained.

ApDhS 2.1.2.6: A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who is accused of being a thief is, after death, born for a limited time in hell; once he has emerged from there, he is born as a Cāṇḍāla if he was a Brāhmaṇa, a Paulkasa if he was a Rājanya, and a Vaiṇa if he was a Vaiśya. ApDhS 2.1.2.7: By other actions that result in the fruit of sin, those who have fallen away are born in wombs that result in the fruit of sin, leading to the loss of their caste.
ApDhS 2.1.2.8: Just as there is a fault in touching, conversing with, or looking at a *caṇḍāla*, so too is there an expiation for that [fault].

ApDhS 2.1.2.9: For touching [water], the expiation is immersion in water; for conversing, conversing with a Brāhmaṇa; and for looking, looking at the luminaries. ApDhS 2.2.3.1: Noble persons, being pure, should be the preparers of the food for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
One should avoid food while facing someone who is speaking, coughing, or sneezing.
Having touched one's hair, limbs, or clothing, one should touch water.
Alternatively, Śūdras supervised by Āryas may act as preparers of the food.
ApDhS 2.2.3.5: For them, the same rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies.
ApDhS 2.2.3.6: In addition, there is the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails every day.
ApDhS 2.2.3.7: And there is the ritual bathing with water together with the wearing of a garment.

Alternatively, they may sow [the seeds] on the eighth days or on the festival days (parvan). Having prepared food out of sight and placed it over the fire, one should sprinkle it with water; that is called the "divine purifier" (devapavitra).
Ap2.2.3.10: When the food is ready, [the wife], standing [there], should announce to the master, "It is prepared.
Ap2.2.3.11: The response is, "May that well-prepared *virāj* food not diminish for me.
Ap2.2.3.12: Whatever offerings and oblations (*bali*) of the householders' food are connected with heaven and prosperity [should be performed].
(K for householders) Ap2.2.3.13: When these mantras are employed, there shall be sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and avoidance of pungent and salty food for twelve days.
Ap2.2.3.14: For the last [mantra], there is a fast for one night.

Ap2.2.3.15: For each of the offerings, the consecration at its respective place consists of wiping with the hand, sprinkling water, and placing it down; afterwards follows the sprinkling around. Ap2.2.3.16: At the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire, one should offer oblations with the hand using the first six formulas, reciting each mantra individually.
Ap2.2.3.17: There is sprinkling around both before and after, as previously described.

Ap2.2.3.18: In this manner, for offerings made at various locations [when they are brought together], there is a single final sprinkling of water at the end. Ap2.2.3.19: When [the offering] is well-mixed, [the rites] should be performed. Ap2.2.3.20:
To the west of the fire, with the seventh and eighth [formulas], [the offering] is made ending toward the north.
Ap2.2.3.21: With the ninth [offering], he offers in the vicinity of the water-vessel.
Ap2.2.3.22: In the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh [offerings], ending toward the east.
Ap2.2.3.23: In the north-eastern part of the house, with the four following [offerings].
(K in the north-eastern region) Ap2.2.4.1/ [One should offer] in the place of the bed with a word indicative of desire.
Ap2.2.4.2/ On the threshold with a word indicative of the intermediate space.
Ap2.2.4.3: With the next [verse], he should place [the vessel] upon the lid. Ap2.2.4.4: With the following [verses], he should place it in the seat of the Brahman priest.

Ap2.2.4.5: To the south, with a formula containing the word "father" (pitṛ-liṅga), wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and with his palm turned downwards, he should perform [the rite].
Ap2.2.4.6: The subsequent [oblation] is for Rudra, as in the case of the [other] deities.
Ap2.2.4.7: For those two, the sprinkling around is separate because of the difference in their ritual characteristics (*dharma*).
Ap2.2.4.8: At night alone, with the final [verse], [the offering] is made into the air (*vaihāyasa*).
Ap2.2.4.9: He who performs these [rites] constantly, without distraction and according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity.
Ap2.2.4.10: And the first portion must be given.
Ap2.2.4.11: One should feed the guests first.
Children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, and women who are pregnant—[these should not be turned away].
At the proper time, the two masters should not refuse one who seeks food.
In the absence of other provisions, [one should offer] land, water, grass, or kind words.
"Indeed, these [gifts] in the house of a virtuous man are never exhausted.
(ApDhS 2.2.4.15) "For one who conducts himself thus, there are infinite worlds.
(ApDhS 2.2.4.16) "To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Veda], a seat, water, and food should be given."
One should not rise [to greet them].
(ApDhS 2.2.4.17) One should rise only for the sake of saluting, provided that one is to be saluted;
this applies to both a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya as well. (ApDhS 2.2.4.18)
ApDhS 2.2.4.19: One should employ a Śūdra who has arrived as a guest in manual labor;
then one should give him food.
ApDhS 2.2.4.20: Or, having brought slaves from the royal household, they should honor the Śūdra like a guest.
Ap2.2.4.21: An upper garment must always be worn. (K 22) Ap2.2.4.22: Or else, a sacred thread (*sūtra*) alone may serve the purpose of the *upavīta*.

(K 23) Ap2.2.4.23: Where food has been eaten, that place should be swept, cleared away, and sprinkled with water; having scraped off the residues from the vessels and mixed them with water, one should offer them to Rudra in a pure spot to the north.
[He should lead it away;
thus the site becomes auspicious.
(K 24) But a Brāhmaṇa is traditionally remembered as the teacher. (K 25)
ApDhS 2.2.4.25: In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may study under a Rājanya or a Vaiśya. ApDhS 2.2.4.26: And he must follow behind them.
ApDhS 2.2.4.27: Thereafter, when they proceed, the Brāhmaṇa alone shall go at the head.

Ap2.2.5.1: Having commenced the study of any of the Upaniṣads among all branches of knowledge, there shall be no study on that day. Ap2.2.5.2: And having studied them, one must not depart immediately. Ap2.2.5.3: However, if he should be in haste, he may go at his pleasure after studying the portion of the Veda intended for the teacher’s inspection.
In this way, there is welfare for both.

(K omits /) If the teacher should arrive after the student has completed his studies (*samāvṛtta*), the student, having approached him face-to-face and having grasped his feet, should touch water without feeling disgust; having placed him in front and attended upon him, he should honor him according to the instruction.

Ap2.2.5.5: When sitting, lying down, eating, drinking, or wearing a garment, he should adopt a more humble manner of conduct when in the presence of his teacher. Ap2.2.5.6: Standing, supporting the teacher with his left hand, he should cause him to sip water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana).
Ap2.2.5.7: Or he may cause another person of equal status to do so.
When one wishes to emulate [the conduct of] standing, sitting, walking, or smiling, [one should do so in their presence].

When they are nearby, one should avoid passing urine, excrement, or wind; speaking loudly, laughing, spitting, gnashing teeth, yawning, frowning, clapping, and blowing the nose. Regarding his wife and children, he should avoid touching them or speaking to them with excessive familiarity.

One should avoid contradicting a teacher’s statement with one’s own statement; likewise, one should avoid contradicting the statements of those who are superior. One should also avoid censuring or reviling any living being.
And by means of one branch of knowledge, he should master the branches of knowledge.
(ApDhS 2.2.5.14) By whichever branch of knowledge he may not shine, he should approach his teacher again and accomplish it through disciplined practice.
(ApDhS 2.2.5.15) From the commencement until the conclusion of the term, the teacher is bound by these observances. (ApDhS 2.2.5.16)
One should avoid shaving the hair, eating meat, performing a *śrāddha*, and sexual intercourse; or one may engage in sexual intercourse with one's wife during her season.
Ap2.2.5.18: He should be devoted to the transmission of knowledge to his pupils according to tradition and to the observances of discipline.
Conducting himself thus, he secures for himself and his ancestors and descendants a state of well-being.

Ap2.2.5.19: By means of the mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, and by restraining the functions of the skin, the generative organ, and the stomach from discharging their secretions, one becomes fit for immortality.

Ap2.3.6.1. When there is doubt regarding a person’s birth or conduct for the sake of determining their religious status (*dharma*), one should kindle the fire that has arrived and inquire about his birth and conduct.
Ap2.3.6.2. If he declares his integrity—saying, "Fire is the witness, wind is the listener, and the sun is the observer;
I declare my integrity"—one should say, "May integrity be with us; this sin is false," and then proceed to instruct him.
ApDhS 2.3.6.3: A guest approaches like a blazing fire. ApDhS 2.3.6.4: Having studied even a single branch of each of the Vedas according to the sacred law, one becomes a *śrotriya*.
Ap2.3.6.5: One who approaches a householder engaged in his own duty, honoring the Law (dharma) and having no other motive, becomes a guest (*atithi*).
Ap2.3.6.6: In honoring him, there is peace and heaven.
Ap2.3.6.7: Having gone out to meet him face-to-face and approached according to age, one should offer him a seat.
Ap2.3.6.8: Some say that when one has the physical capacity, there should be no sitting with the feet together.
Ap2.3.6.9: One should wash his feet;
some say a Śūdra couple [should do so].
At the consecration, one of the two [should act] as the officiant. Some say that one should cause water to be brought for him in an earthen vessel.
One should not cause [the officiant] to sip water.
[One who has not returned from his teacher's house] (K) should cause [the guest] to eat.
Ap2.3.6.13: And here, the completion of one’s Vedic study is also a qualification.
Ap2.3.6.14: Having consoled [him], he should satisfy him with flavorful foods, edibles, and water—at least to a minimum extent.
Ap2.3.6.15: [He should give] a dwelling place, including a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and ointment.
Ap2.3.6.16: Having summoned the preparer of the food, he should pour out rice or barley for that purpose.
Ap2.3.6.17: He should look at the food that has been served, saying, "Let this be more, let that be more.
Ap2.3.6.18: He should say, "Serve more.

Ap2.3.6.19: One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who is hated by him; nor should he eat the food of one who suspects him of a fault, or of one who has been suspected of a fault.
"For he consumes his evil," so it is known.

This very sacrifice of the householder belongs to Prajāpati; it is perpetually extended. That fire which is for guests is the Āhavanīya; that which is in the household is the Gārhapatya; and that on which food is cooked is the Anvāhāryapacana.
"Strength, nourishment, offspring, cattle, and the merit of sacrifices and charitable works"—thus [it is said regarding] the house [of one who eats before the guest].

(ApDhS 2.3.7.3) Food with a libation of milk is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; with clarified butter, it is equal to the Ukthya; with honey, it is equal to the Atirātra; with meat, it is equal to the Dvādaśāha;
and with water, there is an increase of progeny and longevity. (ApDhS 2.3.7.4)
Ap2.3.7.5: It is known from tradition that dear and even unpleasant guests cause one to go to the heavenly world.
Ap2.3.7.6: When he gives [food] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, these become the very Soma-pressings (savana). Ap2.3.7.7:
What he performs [thereby] is indeed the ritual conclusion (udavasyati).
That which he conciliates is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the praise;
that which he accomplishes are the strides of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇukrama*).
"Whatever he turns toward is the *avabhṛtha*," for so says the Brāhmaṇa.
If a guest should arrive when the King is present, he should have a more excellent honor shown to him than to himself.
Ap2.3.7.13: If a guest should arrive when the sacred fires have been established, the host himself should rise to meet him and say: "O Vrātya, where did you stay?
"O Vrātya, [here is] water."
"O Vrātya, satisfying [the gods] with 'tvā'—
thus he should mutter softly before the offering of the Agnihotra:
'O Vrātya, may it be according to your mind.'"
"O Vrātya, let it be as your will; O Vrātya, let it be as your pleasure;
O Vrātya, let it be as your desire."

Ap2.3.7.15: If a guest should arrive when the fires have been taken out but not yet offered, he himself should rise to meet him and say, "O Vratya, grant me permission; I shall offer. Only when permission has been granted should he offer. If he should offer without permission, the Brāhmaṇa declares that there is a fault.
ApDhS 2.3.7.16: "If one should lodge guests for one night, he conquers the earthly worlds; by a second night, the intermediate worlds;

by a third, the celestial worlds; by a fourth, the distant worlds; and by an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds—so it is known. ApDhS 2.3.7.17: "If a guest who is not well-versed in the Vedas should arrive claiming to be such, one should give him a seat, water, and food with the thought: 'I am giving this to a learned śrotriya.'"
In this way, his [prosperity] becomes abundant.

ApDhS 2.4.8.1: One should not rise up for or descend from one's seat to greet a guest who has already been greeted by someone else before him. ApDhS 2.4.8.2: He should eat only the remnants of what remains after the guests have eaten. ApDhS 2.4.8.3: He should not consume flavorful foods in his house without leaving a portion for the guests.

One should not cook choice food for one's own sake alone. A student who has completed his Vedic studies is worthy of the cow, honey, and *madhuparka* offering; so too are the teacher, the officiating priest, the *snātaka*, and a king who is righteous.
ApDhS 2.4.8.7: To the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king, a cow and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) are offered when they visit after a full year has passed.
ApDhS 2.4.8.8: The honey-mixture consists of curds mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey. ApDhS 2.4.8.9:
In the absence of these, water [is offered].

ApDhS 2.4.8.10: The Veda has six ancillaries (aṅgas). ApDhS 2.4.8.11: These are prosody (chandas), ritual science (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), astronomy (jyotiṣa), etymology (nirukta), phonetics (śīkṣā), and the analysis of meters (chando-viciti). ApDhS 2.4.8.12: However, the term "Veda" applies to the collection of rituals that have words and meanings as their basis, upon the completion of the traditional recitation (samāmnāya).
In that regard, the enumeration is contradictory;
however, it is the consensus of those learned in the principles (*nyāyavid*) that the subsidiaries are not designated by the name of the primary acts.
Having rejected a guest, if one remembers him after the meal has been served, one should stop eating from that point and fast.
On the following day, having gratified [the ancestors] according to his inclination, he should perform the final rites;
for one who possesses a vehicle, [he should do so] as far as the vehicle extends.

Ap2.4.9.3: Until the other grants permission; Ap2.4.9.4: In case of a failure to reach an agreement regarding the boundary, he should desist; Ap2.4.9.5: At the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should make all beings, down to the dogs and the Cāṇḍālas, sharers in the offering.
(From dogs and Caṇḍālas) Ap2.4.9.6: Some say that one should not give [food] to those who are unworthy.
Ap2.4.9.7: One who has been initiated (upetaḥ) should avoid the leavings of women and of one who has not been initiated.
Ap2.4.9.8: All gifts are preceded by the offering of water.

Ap2.4.9.9: In the sacrificial enclosure, it is according to the revealed scripture (Śruti). Ap2.4.9.10: A distribution [of food] is ordained for those who are permanent residents and dependent on others, provided it does not cause them hardship.
One may, at will, cause distress to oneself, one's wife, or one's son, but never to a slave or a laborer.
Furthermore, one should act so as not to cause distress to oneself that it renders one incapable of performing one's duties. (K: so as to remain capable of performing one's duties.)
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Eight mouthfuls are the meal for a sage (*muni*); sixteen for a forest-dweller;
thirty-two for a householder; and an unlimited amount for a student (*brahmacārin*). (The items to be eaten.)
"One who has maintained the sacred fires, an ox, and a student of sacred knowledge—these three succeed only while eating; for them there is no success while fasting."

ApDhS 2.5.10.1: The occasions for begging are: when one is a teacher, at a wedding, at a sacrifice, when one's parents desire to support [one], or when there is a lapse in the observances of an Arhat.
ApDhS 2.5.10.2: In those cases, having considered one's qualities, one should give according to one's ability.
ApDhS 2.5.10.3: However, begging for the sake of gratifying the senses is not a valid occasion.
One should not disregard that.

(K 3+4) The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts, inheriting, gleaning ears of grain, and picking up single grains. (K 5) And anything else that has not been specifically forbidden. (K 6)

ApDhS 2.5.10.6: For a Kṣatriya, these same occupations—teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts—are permitted, with the addition of wielding the rod of punishment and fighting. ApDhS 2.5.10.7: For a Vaiśya, as for a Kṣatriya, these are permitted with the exception of wielding the rod of punishment and fighting, but with the addition of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. ApDhS 2.5.10.8: One should not appoint as a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*) one who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who haggles over his fee.
ApDhS 2.5.10.9: One who is ineligible for sacrifice and one who does not study the Veda [are not to be killed].

ApDhS 2.5.10.10: Regarding battle, one should act according to the methods they teach for those engaged in it. ApDhS 2.5.10.11: Noble men declare that the killing of those who have laid down their weapons, whose hair is disheveled, who join their palms in supplication, or who have turned their backs [in flight], is forbidden.

Ap2.5.10.12: For those who have acquired knowledge through the scriptures but have fallen into error due to the weakness of their senses, the teacher should prescribe an expiation according to the specific act, as has been declared.

Ap2.5.10.13: If they should persist in transgressing that scriptural injunction, he should cause them to go before the king. Ap2.5.10.14: The king [should send them] to the domestic priest who is skilled in matters of dharma and artha.

He shall employ Brāhmaṇas [for this purpose]. According to the degree of the offense, he shall cause them to wither away through restrictive penances, excluding corporal punishment or slavery. Regarding the other castes, the king, having considered their actions, shall inflict punishment until the end of their lives.
And one should not inflict punishment when there is doubt.
Having investigated thoroughly until divine tests have been performed, the king may proceed to inflict punishment.
A king who conducts himself in this manner conquers both worlds.
ApDhS 2.5.11.5: The path belongs to the king, except when meeting a Brahmin.
ApDhS 2.5.11.6: But when meeting, the path belongs to the Brahmin alone.
ApDhS 2.5.11.7: The way must be yielded by everyone to one in a vehicle, one burdened with a load, one who is ill, and a woman.
And [the property] of those of higher castes [shall not be taken] by members of other castes.
[However,] for the sake of one's own welfare, [food] must be given by all [castes] to those who are undisciplined, outcasts, intoxicated, or insane.
Through the practice of dharma, a lower caste attains each successive higher caste during the transformation of birth.
ApDhS 2.5.11.11: Through unrighteous conduct, a man of a higher caste descends to each successively lower caste during the transformation of his birth.
ApDhS 2.5.11.12: When one has a wife who is endowed with both virtue and offspring, he should not take another.
ApDhS 2.5.11.13: In the absence of either of these, another may be taken before the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).
For when the *ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires) has been performed, one becomes connected with those rites of which this [fire] is an auxiliary.
One should not give one's daughter to a man of the same *gotra*,
nor to one who is related to her mother through the womb.

In the Brāhma marriage, having ascertained the kinship, character, learning, and health [of the bridegroom], one should bestow the daughter— having adorned her according to one's means— for the sake of offspring, companionship, and religious duties.
In the Ārṣa marriage, a pair of cattle should be given to the father of the daughter.
In the Daiva marriage, one should bestow the bride upon the officiating priest during the course of a sacrifice.
When two people unite with each other out of mutual desire, that is the Gāndharva marriage.

If one should marry after giving away goods within the scope of one's means, that is the Āsura form. If one should marry after causing the father of the daughter to be wearied by labor, that is the Rākṣasa form.

(One should marry after having proclaimed them). 2.5.12.3: Of these, the first three are commendable; each preceding one is superior to the next. 2.5.12.4: As the marriage is constituted, so the offspring becomes constituted.

(Kyathāyukta) Ap2.5.12.5: One should not step upon what has been swept with the hand by a Brāhmaṇa unless it has been sprinkled with water. Ap2.5.12.6–7: One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa.
And having obtained the permission of Brāhmaṇas, he may pass by them;
he should not carry fire and water simultaneously.
One should avoid the simultaneous bringing together of various fires.
One should not circumambulate an Agni being brought forward while it is facing oneself and has not yet been established upon the ground.
And he should not let his hands touch each other behind his back.
If he falls asleep while the sun is setting, he should remain seated for the night without eating and with his speech restrained.
When morning has come, having touched water, he should release his speech.
ApDhS 2.5.12.14: Having slept, or having risen [at dawn], or having failed to eat, or having spoken in an uncontrolled manner, one should remain standing during the day.
ApDhS 2.5.12.15: Some say that one should restrain the breath until sunset. ApDhS 2.5.12.16: Or [one should do so] after seeing a bad dream.
Or [one may perform it] desiring to accomplish a specific purpose; or when there is another transgression of a restrictive rule;
or when there is doubt regarding the result being a fault—it should not be performed in those cases.
ApDhS 2.5.12.20: Likewise regarding days of study and non-study. ApDhS 2.5.12.21:
In a case of doubt, one should not speak as if it were perceived directly. ApDhS 2.5.12.22:

[One should not eat] in the presence of those who have been eclipsed by the sun at sunset or sunrise, those with deformed nails, those with black teeth, the younger brother whose elder brother is married before him (didhiṣūpati), the elder brother whose younger brother is married before him (paryāhita), the younger brother whose elder brother has taken a second wife while the first is still living (parīṣṭa), the elder brother whose younger brother has taken a second wife while the first is still living (parivitta), the younger brother whose elder brother has taken a second wife while the first is still living (parivinna), and the elder brother whose younger brother has taken a second wife while the first is still living (parivividāna).
In each successive case among these four, the penance for performing an impure act becomes increasingly more severe.
And that sign, some say, should be removed after having performed the penance.

ApDhS 2.6.13.1: For those who approach a woman of the same caste who has been previously authorized by scripture according to the proper season, there is a connection with their sons through their ritual duties.
ApDhS 2.6.13.2: And there is no deviation regarding the inheritance for both [the father and the son].
ApDhS 2.6.13.3: There is fault in sexual intercourse with one who has not been previously authorized (*asaṃskṛtā*), or with a woman of a different caste.
In that case as well, the son alone is the one who bears the fault.
For there is a Brāhmaṇa text stating, "The son belongs to the progenitor.
Furthermore, they cite this:
O Janaka, it is only now that I envy women, and not before;
for when they spoke of the son in the abode of Yama as belonging to the progenitor.
The depositor of seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the seed of another, they guard their wives.
"Be vigilant and guard this lineage; let no one sow the seeds of another in your field.
In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; the sower merely makes this lineage in vain."
Transgression of the Law and acts of violence are seen among the ancients.
Because of their extraordinary spiritual power (*tejas*), no sin (*pratyavāya*) attaches to them.
An inferior person who, having observed that, applies such conduct, perishes.

There is no such thing as giving away or selling a child. Regarding marriage, it is heard in the sacred texts that a gift to the father of the daughter is optional; for the sake of merit, it is prescribed that "one hundred [cows] plus a chariot should be given to the father of the daughter," and one should not perform this falsely.
In that context, the word "purchase" (kraya) is merely figurative praise.

For the connection [of the inheritance] is based on the law (dharma). (ApDhS 2.6.13.12) Having satisfied the eldest son with a single share of the property, he should, while still living, divide the inheritance among his sons equally, excluding one who is impotent, insane, or an outcast. (ApDhS 2.6.14.1)
In the absence of a son, the nearest *sapiṇḍa* shall perform the rites;
in his absence, the teacher; and in the absence of the teacher, the pupil, having taken the property, shall employ it for the sake of those purposes or for religious duties.
Or, the daughter may do so.
ApDhS 2.6.14.5: In the absence of all [heirs], the king shall take the inheritance.
ApDhS 2.6.14.6: Some say that the eldest son alone is the heir.
ApDhS 2.6.14.7: In certain regions, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest.
The chariot and the household utensils belong to the father;
the ornaments and the wealth of kinsmen belong to the wife— so say some.
That is contradicted by the scriptures.
It is heard in the Veda without qualification that "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons";
yet it is also heard as if it were a singular case that "therefore they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth."

Moreover, those who know the principles of reasoning say that even an eternal restatement (*nityānuvāda*) is not an injunction (*avidhi*), as in the cases: "Therefore, goats and sheep move together among domestic animals"; "Therefore, the mouth of a *snātaka* seems to resound"; and "Therefore, the goat and the Vedic scholar are most desirous of women."
For all those who are endowed with righteousness are sharers [in the reward].
But if even the eldest distributes goods through unrighteous means, one should deprive him of his share. No division of property exists between husband and wife;
for from the time of the taking of the hand, they possess joint status in religious rites.
Likewise regarding the fruits of merit, the acquisition of property,
and gifts given on specific occasions during the absence of the master, they do not declare such acts to be theft.
ApDhS 2.6.15.1: By this, the customs of regions and families are explained.

ApDhS 2.6.15.2: For those related to the mother through the womb and for those related to the father up to the seventh generation, or as long as the relationship is known—if they have died, one should perform the touching of water (libation) for them, excluding those who were in the womb and those who have not yet reached one year of age.
Among these, the mother and father alone [are the primary objects of veneration];
so too are those who take [one's property].
When one’s wife has died or when a supreme guru has passed away, there shall be fasting at improper times.
(K and *akālabhojana*) Ap2.6.15.6:
They should prepare the condiments for the sick.
Ap2.6.15.7–8: Having scattered their hair and strewn dust [over themselves], they should be clad in a single garment. (Is it "having strewn dust and being clad in a single garment"?)
Facing south, they immerse themselves once, emerge, and sit down;
thus three times. (Having poured [the water], they wear a single garment.)
2: Having stirred it up, 3: *oṃ*. 4:
[K 8 adds] "Thus three times. Ap2.6.15.9: Having splashed water toward that [deceased] with conviction, they return to the village without looking back; whatever the women say, they do that.
Regarding other [occasions], some teachers prescribe this very same [procedure].
(ApDhS 2.6.15.10) One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual acts.
(ApDhS 2.6.15.11) He establishes that gifts are to be bestowed according to place, time, purity, and the propriety of the recipient. (ApDhS 2.6.15.12)

Ap2.6.15.13: That which is not prepared in one's own fire, and that from which no portion is first offered, must not be eaten. Ap2.6.15.14: An oblation consisting of alkaline substances or salt is not prescribed. Ap2.6.15.15: Likewise, there is no [oblation] for those of lower status, nor for that which has been mixed [with such].

Ap2.6.15.16: For the offering of non-sacrificial food, one should remove the hot ashes toward the north and offer it therein; that becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. Ap2.6.15.17: A woman should not offer the oblation. Ap2.6.15.18: Nor should one who has not been initiated.
Until the first feeding with solid food, embryos do not become impure.
Some say until one full year has passed;
others say as long as they would not recognize the directions.
"Until the initiation ceremony (upanayana)," says another [teacher]. For it is at this point that one gains the entitlement to the sacred scriptures;
that constitutes the completion [of the preliminary stage].
And there is also the Smṛti:
"In former times, gods and humans existed together in this world.
Then, by means of their ritual acts (*karma*), the gods went to heaven, while humans were left behind."
Among them, those who undertake such actions together with the gods and Brahmā exist in that world.
Now, Manu has declared this rite by the word *śrāddha*, and it serves for the supreme welfare of progeny. (1+2 = K 1)
In that rite, the ancestors are the deities, while the Brahmins serve the purpose of the Āhavanīya fire.
It is to be performed month after month.

The latter part of the afternoon of the dark fortnight is superior. Likewise, the later days of the dark fortnight are [more] excellent. By performing [the rite] on any day whatsoever during the dark fortnight, one gratifies the ancestors.
But due to the restriction regarding the time of performance, there is a distinction in the result:
(K 6) if it is performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born; (K 7) if on the second day, they are thieves; (K 8) if on the third day, they are prone to disease.
In the third [year], they possess spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*);
(K 9) in the fourth, they possess small livestock;
(K 10) in the fifth, they have male children.

He has many offspring and does not die childless. (ApDhS 2.7.16.13) In the sixth year, he becomes habituated to long journeys and to gambling with dice. (ApDhS 2.7.16.14) In the seventh year, there is success in agriculture. (ApDhS 2.7.16.15)
In the eighth [month], there is nourishment;
(K 14) in the ninth, single-hoofed animals;
(K 15) in the tenth, success in legal proceedings. (K 16)
In the eleventh year, he becomes one who possesses black iron, tin, and lead.
In the twelfth year, he becomes possessed of cattle.
In the thirteenth year, he has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring.
But those who die young [occur];
(Ap2.7.16.21) success in weaponry occurs on the fourteenth; (Ap2.7.16.22) nourishment occurs on the fifteenth. (Ap2.7.16.23)
In that regard, the substances are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, roots, and fruits.
(K 22) But when the food is oily, the gratification of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a longer period.
(K 23) Likewise, it is so when the substance has been acquired through righteous means and offered at a sacred place. (K 24)
For one year, there is satisfaction through beef;
for a longer period than that, through buffalo meat.
By this, the sacrificial purity of the meat of domestic and wild animals is explained.
Ap2.7.17.1: With the meat of the rhinoceros served on a bed of rhinoceros meat, one attains an infinite duration of time.
Ap2.7.17.2: Likewise with the meat of the *śatabali* fish. Ap2.7.17.3: And likewise with the meat of the *vārdhrāṇasa*.
(K vārghrāṇasa) Ap2.7.17.4:
Being self-restrained, serene in mind, and invited, he should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or residence as a pupil.
Ap2.7.17.5: However, if others lack superior qualities, even a uterine brother who possesses them should be fed.
By this, the resident pupils are explained.
Now, they also cite this example:
"The *saṃbhojanī*—the alms-food of the Piśācas—goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods."
Right here she wanders, her merit exhausted, like a cow that has lost its calf within the stalls. Right here, consuming [the offerings] from family to family, the sacrificial gift perishes.
Among those of equal qualities, one who is older in age is superior, as is one who is destitute of wealth if he desires [the honor].
On the day before, there is the announcement;
on the following day, the second [announcement].
ApDhS 2.7.17.13: There is a third invitation.
ApDhS 2.7.17.14: Some teach that the *śrāddha* consists of three preliminary offerings (*prāya*).
ApDhS 2.7.17.15: As the first [offering] is performed, so too are the second and the third.
In all [ritual] procedures, having taken portions from all [the sacrificial foods] together, he should eat of the remainder at least one mouthful, as previously prescribed.
(K: *grāsa-varārdhyam*) (*ed.:
*avarārghyam*)
But according to the practice of the northerners, when those seated on mats have water-vessels brought to their hands, he addresses them:
"Let [the food] be removed," and "Let [the oblation] be made in the fire.
If they give permission, saying, "Let it be removed at will" and "Let it be made in the fire at will," he may remove the food and offer the oblation.
They declare that the sight of dogs and outcastes at a *śrāddha* is censurable.

A leper, one who is deformed, one who approaches the bed of another, the son of a soldier, and one born of a *śūdra* woman by a Brāhmaṇa—these, while eating at a *śrāddha*, become defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaṇa*).

One who knows the *trimadhu*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *triṇāciketa*; one who has performed the four *medha* sacrifices; one who maintains the five sacred fires; one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who has studied the Veda; and the son of a learned man (*anūcāna*) who is himself a *śrotriya*—these, while eating at a *śrāddha*...
They are purifiers of the assembly.
(The master of the eldest son is the one who presides.
One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night.
ApDhS 2.7.17.24: And once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion.
ApDhS 2.7.17.25: Except in the case of an eclipse of the moon.

One should avoid melted butter (vilayana), churned curds (mathita), oil-cake (piṇyāka), honey, and meat; as well as black grains, the food of a Śūdra, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten by others.

Ap2.8.18.3: One who desires memory, fame, intelligence, heaven, and prosperity should avoid these twelve things for a year: food unfit for sacrifice, untruth, anger, and that which causes anger. Ap2.8.18.4:

Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three periods of the day, subsisting on food not cooked by fire, avoiding the shade of others, and remaining mostly standing or sitting, he should observe this for a year.
One should observe this vow;
they call this the forty-eight-fold [observance].
