One should give those items by which the food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten to those who have already eaten;
one should also feed those who have risen together [with the guests].
And one should not give the leavings to someone who does not possess those qualities.
In this manner for a year.
For them, the final rite should be performed with a copper goat.
He should have a measuring-vessel prepared that is covered.
(K 15) He should feed the Brāhmaṇas in its northern half.
(K 16) They teach that he beholds both: the Brāhmaṇas while they are eating, and the ancestors in the measuring-vessel. (K 17)
Ap2.8.18.17: From this point forward, [the rite] is both performed and unperformed.
Ap2.8.18.18: For by means of the *śrāddha*, the ancestors indeed experience satisfaction.
Ap2.8.18.19: One who desires prosperity should perform the rite under the asterism Tiṣya.

Ap2.8.19.1: Having had the flour of white mustard seeds prepared, he should wash his hands and feet with them, rinse his mouth and ears, and then sit where the wind does not blow strongly; the skin of a goat is the first choice for a seat.
Restraining his speech and facing south, he should eat;
however, they teach that eating while facing such a direction is detrimental to the life-span of one's mother.
A cup made of Udumbara wood with a golden base is prescribed for the *praśāstṛ*.
And it must not be used by anyone else.
[He should] bring [the food] in mouthfuls; [he should] not let it spill; he should not leave anything behind.
Or he should expel it.
He should swallow the entire morsel together with the thumb.
One should not make a sound with the mouth;
one should not shake the hand;
and having sipped water, one should hold the hands raised until they become wet.
Then he should touch fire;
(K 9) he should not eat during the day, except for roots and fruits; (K 10) and he should avoid those things intended as portions for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice. (K 11)
He should eat while wearing his upper garment over the left shoulder as a sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*) and with an upper covering.
(ApDhS 2.8.19.16) But at the *nitya* Śrāddha, he should provide food that contains oil.
(ApDhS 2.8.19.17) Ghee and meat constitute the primary rule. (ApDhS 2.8.19.18)

In the absence [of sesame], oil may be used as a vegetable substitute. (ApDhS 2.8.19.19) And under the Maghā asterism, one should feed the Brahmins with clarified butter according to the ritual rules for a Śrāddha.
(ApDhS 2.8.19.20) At the monthly Śrāddha, one should employ a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds by whatever means possible that one is able to provide. (ApDhS 2.8.20.1)
Ap2.8.20.2: He should feed those who have risen together [in learning], and they should not give the remains of the meal to one who does not possess those same qualities.

Ap2.8.20.3: During the northern course of the sun, in the fortnight of the waxing moon, having fasted for at least one night, one desiring prosperity should cook a *sthālīpāka* under the asterism Tiṣya; having sacrificed to Mahārāja and fed a Brāhmaṇa with that [food] mixed with clarified butter, he should proceed.
For the sake of nourishment, he should cause the *siddhi* to be recited; thus day by day until the last *tiṣya* constellation. On the second day, two [recitations].
Three on the third day;
thus for a year,
by this accumulation, he nourishes great prosperity.

ApDhS 2.8.20.9: Fasting must be observed from the very beginning. ApDhS 2.8.20.10: One should avoid eating food from those whose vital energy has been taken away. ApDhS 2.8.20.11: Nor should one stand upon ashes or chaff.
One should avoid washing one foot with the other, standing upon it, swinging the feet,
and resting the shank upon the knee.
And scratching with the nails; (K: scratching);
cracking the joints without cause;
and whatever else they censure.
He who bestows wealth upon those engaged in righteous acts and in the acquisition of property;
he who bestows it at a sacred place (*tīrtha*); and he who restrains it from being spent on what is not a sacred place, provided that no danger should arise therefrom.
He shall gather men to himself; he shall enjoy pleasures that are not forbidden by dharma;
thus he conquers both worlds.

ApDhS 2.9.21.1: There are four stages of life (āśrama): that of the householder, that of the teacher’s family, that of the silent sage, and that of the forest-dweller. ApDhS 2.9.21.2: By conducting oneself without distraction in all of these according to the instructions, one attains security.
ApDhS 2.9.21.3: For all of them, residence in the teacher’s family beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is common.
Ap2.9.21.4: For all [students], there is no relinquishing of their learning.
Ap2.9.21.5: Having understood the ritual acts, he may undertake whatever he desires.

Ap2.9.21.6: Just as there is a rule for one seeking knowledge, by that very same [rule] the student remains until the end; the casting off of the body in the teacher’s household is the duty of the *brahmacārin*.
Now, concerning the wandering mendicant (parivrāja): he departs from this very state while still observing the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). For him, they prescribe [the following]:
He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling; the sage should be without shelter and without refuge.

Abandoning all speech except for his Vedic recitation, and obtaining his livelihood for the sake of sustaining life in a village, he should wander without desire and without looking for the next world.
For him, it is ordained that discarded clothing may serve as a covering.
ApDhS 2.9.21.12: Some say that liberation comes from all sides.

ApDhS 2.9.21.13: Having abandoned truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, the Vedas, and this world as well as the next, one should seek the Self. ApDhS 2.9.21.14: When it is realized, there is the attainment of security.
That is contradicted by the scriptures.
If the attainment of security occurred upon awakening, one would not experience suffering even here in this world.
By this, the subsequent case is also explained.
Now, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha). From this very state, while still observing the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), he goes forth.
Regarding him, they teach as follows:
The sage should have but one fire, be homeless, and remain without shelter or protection,
renouncing all speech except for his private Vedic recitation.
For him, clothing made from forest materials is prescribed.
Then he should subsist on roots, fruits, leaves, and grass; finally, he should subsist on things that have fallen of their own accord. Then he should take refuge in water, air, and space.
Among these, each subsequent stage of union is superior in terms of its fruit.
Alternatively, some teach that for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) alone there is a sequential order:
having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes those ritual acts which are prescribed as being subsequent to the *Soma* sacrifice.

Having built a house, he should dwell outside the village together with his wife, his offspring, and the sacred fires; or he may live alone. He should subsist by gathering ears of grain or by picking up individual grains.
And from this point forward, he should not accept gifts.
Once consecrated, he should offer oblations.
He should descend into the water slowly, striking it gently, and touch the water while facing the sun.
"Ap2.9.22.14: Thus, in all cases, is the rule for touching water. Ap2.9.22.15:
Some teachers prescribe a pair of each of the following articles for the purpose of cooking and eating: a razor, an axe, and a sickle."
(Regarding pairs of objects, for the purpose of cooking or eating:
Having taken one from each of the pairs and given away the others, he should dwell in the forest. (Regarding the pairs.)
From this point forward, his sacrificial oblation, livelihood, receiving of guests, and clothing shall be provided solely from the forest.
In those rites where there are *puroḍāśas* (cake-offerings), they should be made as *carus* (boiled rice-oblations).
And everything, including the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Ap2.9.22.20: One should not call out toward the forest.
Ap2.9.22.21: A shelter for the sake of the fire.
Ap2.9.22.22: [The fire] itself in the open air.
[He should use] a bed and seat that are not spread with grass. When new grain has been obtained, he may consume the old grain.
Or, desiring a more extensive discipline, he should fetch his daily sustenance every day with a vessel in the evening and in the morning.

Thereafter, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses, he should practice; finally, he should resort to flowing water, then to air, and then to space. Among these, each subsequent stage is superior in its result.
[It is] distinguished.
(K inserts /) Ap2.9.23.3. Now, they cite two verses from the Purāṇas:
Ap2.9.23.4. (Ś) "The eighty-eight thousand sages who were masters of progeny..."
To the south, those eighty-eight thousand seers who did not desire offspring have taken their place in the cremation grounds along the path of Aryaman;
to the north, they attain immortality along the path of Aryaman.
Ap2.9.23.6: Thus ends the praise of those who maintain their vital energy upwards (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Ap2.9.23.7: Furthermore, there are also those for whom success is achieved through mere intention (*saṃkalpa*).
Ap2.9.23.8: Such as bringing rain, granting offspring, seeing at a distance, moving with the speed of thought, and whatever else is similarly appropriate.

(= K 7, *prajā-dānam*) Therefore, because their fruits are directly perceived and because of the Vedic revelation, some declare these stages of life (*āśrama*) to be superior. (= K 8) But for those who are advanced in the three Vedas, the Vedas themselves are the ultimate authority; therein lie those [injunctions] which are heard.

They consider conduct that contradicts those rules—concerning rice, barley, livestock, clarified butter, milk, the sacrificial potsherds, and the connection with the wife—which must be performed loudly or softly, to be invalid.
(K 11) Furthermore, as for what is called the "cremation ground," this is prescribed as the final purification of the person at the conclusion of various rites. (K 12)
Beyond that, an infinite fruit denoted by the word "heaven" is heard [in scripture].
Moreover, the sacred tradition declares his immortality through progeny:

"Through offspring you are born again; that is your immortality among mortals. Furthermore, this very same person is perceived separately when grown, and a similarity is observed, though the bodily form is indeed different.
Those who abide in the duties prescribed by the learned increase the fame and the heavenly merit of their predecessors in the afterlife;
in this way, each subsequent generation benefits those who preceded them until the dissolution of all beings. Thus, they are conquerors of heaven.
"Furthermore, they become seeds for a new creation," so it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
Moreover, there is the word of Prajāpati:
"The threefold knowledge, the life of celibate study, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts."
"Those who perform these [acts], with them we shall be; having become dust, we perish while praising something else."
Among them, those who have committed evil perish like the leaf of a tree; they do not harm others.
In this world, he has no connection with his actions, and likewise in the next world, he has no connection with the fruits of his actions.
This is to be understood by means of this.
ApDhS 2.9.24.12: This is the creation of Prajāpati and the sages.

ApDhS 2.9.24.13: Among them, those who have performed meritorious deeds are perceived to possess supreme, radiant natures. ApDhS 2.9.24.14: However, by means of a portion of their karma or through austerity, someone may—while still embodied—conquer a finite world and attain the fulfillment of their will; yet this does not constitute the superiority of the stages of life (āśramas).
Ap2.9.25.1: The common and specific duties of all social classes have been explained.
We shall now explain those of the king specifically.
(= K omits /)
The duties of the king:
He should have the palace and the city constructed with a southern gate;
the palace should be located within the inner city.
To the east of that [fortress] is the residence; they call that the place of invitation (*āmantraṇa*).

To the south of the fortress is the assembly hall (*sabhā*), with doors opening to the south and the north, so that both the interior and the exterior are visible. In all [these buildings], the sacred fires must be maintained perpetually.
And the worship of the sacred fire must be performed daily, just as in the domestic ritual.

He should provide lodging for guests who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas) in his residence, starting with those of the lowest rank. To them, dwellings, bedding, food, and drink should be provided according to their merit.
He should not live at the expense of his teachers or ministers.
And in his domain, no one should perish through hunger, disease, cold, or heat, whether due to lack of resources or by intentional neglect.
In the middle of the assembly hall, having raised up a gaming-place and sprinkled it with water, he should cast down an even number of Vibhītaka dice according to their purpose.
Noble men, pure and truthful in character, should be the gamblers. The taking up of weapons, dancing, singing, and instrumental music—these should not exist except under the authority of the king.
A king is a provider of security for whom there is no fear of thieves in his realm, whether in a village or in the forest.

ApDhS 2.10.26.1: By giving land and wealth to Brahmins according to their merit, without causing hardship to his dependents, a king conquers infinite worlds. ApDhS 2.10.26.2: They say that a king who is slain while seeking to recover the property of Brahmins is a sacrifice in which he himself is the sacrificial post and the sacrificial fee is infinite. ApDhS 2.10.26.3: By this, other heroes are also explained—those who, fighting for a righteous cause, lay down their bodies.
In villages and cities, he should appoint noble, pure, and truth-abiding men for the protection of the subjects.
Their attendants should likewise possess those same qualities.
A city extending for one *yojana* in every direction must be protected from thieves.
A *krośa* from the villages;
there, whatever is stolen by them must be made good [by restitution].
He shall cause the lawful toll to be collected.
An unlearned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) who does not know the alphabet; women of all castes;
and boys before their secondary sexual characteristics have appeared.
And those who dwell for the sake of learning;
those ascetics who are devoted to dharma;
and the Śūdra who washes their feet.
And those who are blind, mute, deaf, afflicted by disease, or possessed by spirits;
and those who are useless because they have already acquired wealth—
if such a man, without prior intent, enters another's house while adorned as a youth, or approaches another's wife or a maiden, he shall be restrained by a verbal reprimand.
But if it was done intentionally, one with a wicked disposition shall be punished.
When sexual intercourse has occurred, the penis, along with the testicles, shall be cut off.
In the case of a virgin, however, he shall be stripped of his own property and banished.
Now, [regarding] a servant [who has committed an offense], [the king shall act];
and from this point forward, [he shall act] regarding one who is to be protected from sexual intercourse. However, when a means of atonement has been accepted, he shall release him to his masters.
ApDhS 2.10.27.1: When he has acted according to the rule, his connection with dharma remains as before.

ApDhS 2.10.27.2: He should not disclose to others a woman who stands in the position of a *sagotra* (a female of the same lineage). ApDhS 2.10.27.3: For they teach that a woman is given away for the sake of the family.
That [misconduct] arises from the weakness of the senses. For the status of being "another" (paratva) is no different for one's own hand;
indeed, upon the transgression of that [principle], both [the perpetrator and the victim] go to hell.
For an undertaking based on restrictive observances (*niyama*) leads to a greater spiritual advancement than offspring resulting from such an undertaking.
An Ārya who begets a child upon a Śūdra woman is to be exiled;
a Śūdra who begets a child upon an Ārya woman is to be put to death.
And he should cause his wife to fast.
Regarding sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste who has previously been married to another, they teach that one quarter of a *pātaka* falls [upon him] for a single act;
likewise, for repetition, a quarter falls for each instance.
ApDhS 2.10.27.13: In the fourth [case], everything [is forfeited].
ApDhS 2.10.27.14: The tongue shall be cut out for a Śūdra who reviles a righteous Ārya.
ApDhS 2.10.27.15: For one who encroaches upon another's speech, path, bed, or seat, there shall be a flogging with a rod.
In cases of killing a human, theft, or seizing land, one who has taken these [goods] belonging to another shall be put to death.
However, for a Brāhmaṇa in these cases, there shall be the blinding of the eyes.
Or, he may be bound in secret for violating a rule or for other offenses.
Until the completion [of the offense];
if it is not completed, he is not to be killed.
An Ācārya, an officiating priest (ṛtvij), a Snātaka, and a king—these may provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death.
Ap2.11.28.1: When a field has been taken up for cultivation, if there is no harvest due to a lack of effort, it may be confiscated by one who is prosperous and capable of bringing it to fruition.
Ap2.11.28.2–3: For a dependent laborer (*kīnāśa*) who abandons his work, the punishment is flogging with a rod;
the same applies to a cattle-herder.
And he shall provide an enclosure for his livestock.
Having left the pen at dawn, he shall emaciate the animals but not cause them to perish.
If he has enclosed the animals and they die or are lost, he shall restore them to their owners.

If, through negligence, one sees cattle that have been let loose in the forest, he should bring them to the village and return them to their owners. (K 8) If negligence occurs again, he should pen them up once; beyond that, he need not look after them. (K 9–10)
Ap2.11.28.10: An ignorant man who takes another’s property—whether firewood, water, roots, flowers, fruit, fragrances, food, or vegetables—is to be restrained by a verbal reprimand.

Ap2.11.28.11: For one who knows better, there shall be the confiscation of his clothing. Ap2.11.28.12: One who takes food when his life is in danger is not to be punished, even if he did so intentionally.
ApDhS 2.11.28.13: When the occasion for punishment has arisen, if the king fails to inflict it, sin touches him.
ApDhS 2.11.29.1: The instigator, the advisor, and the doer are sharers in the fruits of actions that lead to heaven or hell. ApDhS 2.11.29.2:
He who contributes most to the undertaking receives the greater portion of the fruit.
The two heads of the household have authority over the wealth. With their consent, others also may manage that property for their benefit.
In case of a dispute, those who are endowed with learning and noble birth, who are aged, wise, and unerring in matters of dharma, shall decide.
In case of doubt, having deliberated according to the signs and by means of divine ordeal,

on an auspicious day in the morning when the fire has been kindled, having caused the oath to be proclaimed both before and after the water-vessel containing the royal insignia (*rājavatī*) in the presence of water, with the permission of all, the principal witness shall state the truthful answer. If he speaks falsely, the king shall inflict punishment.
And in this world, as well as in the life hereafter, hell awaits him;
(but) through truth there is heaven and the praise of all beings. That which is found among women and Śūdras is the ultimate limit of knowledge.
They teach that this is the supplement to the Atharvaveda.
The completion of the dharma is declared to be difficult; however, it is accomplished through the performance of the ritual characteristics as handed down in the tradition.
In this regard, the defining characteristic is as follows:

In all inhabited regions, he should adopt the conduct of those who are exclusively composed, noble, well-disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy— conduct that is consistent with their virtuous way of life.
Thus he conquers both worlds.
Regarding the remaining duties of dharma, some say that one should learn them from women and from members of all social classes—so say some.
And thus the Dharmasūtra of Āpastamba is completed.
